To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

women who gained more weight in pregnancy had lower 24,25(OH)2D in early pregnancy, delivered in winter, or had low compliance with vitamin D supplementation, had lower 24-hydroxyvitamine D in late pregnancy.

the 25-hydroxvitamin D ( 25(OH))D response to vitamin D supplementation during pregnancy is affected by pregnancy weight gain, compliance with study medication, early pregnancy 25 (OH)D, and season at delivery.
women who gained more weight from 14 to34 weeks of gestational age had lower vitamin D levels at 34 weeks in pregnancy, and that women who delivered in the winter had lower vitamin D at 34 weeks.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the determinants of the maternal 25-hydroxylated vitamin D response to antenatal supplementation.
the role of vitamin D in pregnancy and the health of the mother and baby.
the role of vitamin D in the development of chronic diseases in children and adults.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
vitamin D supplementation during pregnancy is not associated with a consistent 25-hydroxyl vitamin D response.

the maternal and environmental characteristics of the study participants, including weight gain during pregnancy, 25(OH)Vitamin D status, season, and compliance with vitamin D supplementation, were associated with the maternal 25(OH)vitamin D response to vitamin D supplementation during pregnancy.

women who gained more weight, had lower 25-hydroxylated vitamin D levels in early pregnancy and who gave birth in the winter achieved lower vitamin D levels when supplemented with 1,000 IU of vitamin D per day.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the 1000 IU of vitamin D daily that we used in this study did not raise the vitamin D levels enough for most pregnant women, and that we need to use more than 1000 IU per day.
the 25-hydroxylase activity is influenced by pregnancy weight gain and season of birth.
we found that the 25-hydroxylase is a very important determinant of vitamin D status in pregnancy and it is important to consider this when designing trials of vitamin D in pregnancy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is considerable variability in the 25(OH)-vitamin D response to vitamin D supplementation during pregnancy.
the 25(OH)vitamin D response to vitamin D supplementation in pregnant women is influenced by a number of maternal and environmental characteristics.
women who gain weight during pregnancy and deliver in winter may need higher doses of vitamin D supplementation to achieve 25(OH)-D repletion during pregnancy.
